title: Grandma’s Pickled Jalapeños

items.raw: 1 pound (450 g) jalapeños, sliced into ¼-inch rings
1 small carrot, sliced into thin coins (optional)
1 cup (240 ml) distilled white vinegar, 5% acidity
1 tablespoon (18 g) pickling or canning salt
½ teaspoon dried oregano, preferably Mexican

steps.text: Wear disposable gloves to slice the peppers, and do not touch your eyes or face. The oils stay on your skin for hours, even after washing.
Slice the jalapeños into ¼-inch rings, discarding the stems. Pack them into a clean quart jar with the carrot, onion, and garlic, layering as you go.
Bring the vinegar, water, salt, sugar, oregano, and bay leaf to a boil in a small saucepan, stirring until the salt and sugar dissolve.
Pour the hot brine straight over the peppers until they are submerged. Pouring it hot onto raw peppers keeps them crisp; simmering them in the brine makes them soft.
Let the jar cool to room temperature, uncovered, then close and refrigerate. They are ready in 24 hours and best after 3 days, when the bright green turns olive.

notes.label: Heat level
notes.text: most of the heat is in the seeds and white ribs. For milder pickles, scrape out some of the seeds before slicing.

notes.label: Storage
notes.text: keep refrigerated and use within 2 months. Always use a clean fork to take them out of the jar.

notes.label: For the pantry
notes.text: to make them shelf-stable, follow a tested canning recipe for pickled hot peppers (USDA or Ball) exactly, including its brine and processing time.

notes.label: Uses
notes.text: nachos, tacos, sandwiches, eggs, or chopped into cornbread batter. The brine is good in a salad dressing.

openQuestion: This is a best guess — sliced jalapeños in a quick refrigerator brine, with optional carrot and onion the way taquerias serve them. Tell me how Grandma made hers: sliced or whole, with carrots or just peppers, sweet or plain, canned or kept in the refrigerator — and what she put them on.
